name: Egypt (New Kingdom, Thutmose III)

territory.border: hb:bc1500:Egypt + hb:bc1500:Kush + hb:bc1500:Kingdom of David and Solomon

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Polity Territory 650,000 km2 for 1500-1451 BCE and 900,000 km2 for 1450-1351 BCE; Taagepera 1978 gives 1.0 million km2 at 1450 BCE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires). Border = historical-basemaps world_bc1500 'Egypt' (Nile valley to ~23 N) + 'Kush' (Nubia to the Fourth Cataract, overreaches south to ~16 N) + 'Kingdom of David and Solomon' (the Levant incl. Megiddo and Kadesh), ~748,000 km2 computed from the GeoJSON.

population.note: Seshat codes 3,350,000-4,500,000 for the Thutmosid New Kingdom (1550-1293 BCE), mid = midpoint. Low: OWID/McEvedy-Jones series (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) gives Egypt 1.5 M in 2000 BCE and 2.0 M in 1000 BCE (~1.75 M at 1450) plus ~0.7 M for Nubia and the Canaanite vassals. High adds the Levantine vassals to the Seshat high.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Egypt was a village society with a few large centres; Seshat codes the largest settlement (Thebes or Memphis) at 30,000-100,000.

activePersonnel.note: Thutmose III's field army at Megiddo (1457 BCE) is estimated at c. 10,800 (Redford 2003 pp. 197-198, cited in the fetched page), with about 1,000 chariots and 10,000 infantry on each side; the Karnak annals list 924 captured chariots. The empire also kept garrisons in Nubia (Buhen and the fortresses) and Canaan (Gaza, Ullaza, Sumur) and home troops. Mid = one field army plus the overseas garrisons and the fleet.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Conscripts and veterans holding land who could be recalled for a summer campaign.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Chariot crews (2 per vehicle, ~2,000), crews of the Levant transport fleet, grooms, scribes and the supply train.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Professionalised army plus conscription of one man in ten from temple estates (later attested) on a large peasant population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Thutmose III's field army at Megiddo (1457 BCE) is estimated at c. 10,800 (Redford 2003 pp. 197-198, cited in the fetched page), with about 1,000 chariots and 10,000 infantry on each side; the Karnak annals list 924 captured chariots. The empire also kept garrisons in Nubia (Buhen and the fortresses) and Canaan (Gaza, Ullaza, Sumur) and home troops. Split: spear-and-shield infantry ~50% of the foot.

quality.note: Bronze spears, khopesh, large shields; good for the era.

training.note: Professional standing army of the 18th dynasty (rubric 0.75) with conscripts.

quality.note: Light two-horse Egyptian chariot with composite-bow archer, among the era's best (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Educated guess. Thutmose III built ships at Byblos for his Euphrates crossing (Year 33) and moved troops by sea to Phoenician harbours each year; war galleys and transports, no count survives.

quality.note: Oared Nile and sea galleys of the era.

training.note: Professional crews of the Peru-nefer naval base.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: Thutmose III ran 16-17 campaigns, chose the risky Aruna pass at Megiddo and won, organised annual seaborne supply; trained officer corps (scribes of recruits).

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: professional army with unit identity; Megiddo victory compromised when troops broke to loot the camp.

weapons.note: Anchor 2 (1400 BCE): composite bow, war chariot, bronze khopesh.

armor.note: Anchor 2: bronze scale for chariot crews; most infantry unarmoured.

ships.note: Anchor 2: oared war galleys, seaborne logistics to the Levant.

fortification.note: Anchor 2: stone and mudbrick Nubian fortresses (Buhen) and Ways of Horus forts.

logistics.note: Anchor 2: depots in Phoenician ports supplied by sea each campaign season.

communications.note: Anchor 2: royal couriers and Levantine vassal correspondence.

isr.note: Year anchor ~1.9: scouts, spies, interrogated prisoners.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Egypt 1 CE = 1,116, 730 CE = 1,164 (2011 int$). New Kingdom Egypt applied slightly below the Roman-era value.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Imperial phase with annual campaigns; booty and tribute offset costs.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Large temple and royal workshops.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Nile flood agriculture produced reliable surpluses stored in state granaries.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. The fortified Ways of Horus coastal road from Tjaru to Gaza (~250 km) and Levantine routes; the Nile was the main artery.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Memphis/Peru-nefer, Thebes, plus Phoenician harbours used as depots (Byblos, Ullaza, Sumur).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Nile cargo boats and Levant sea ships of 10-50 t.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Supported by sea along the Levant coast; inland Syria required pre-stocked depots.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Cattle, donkeys and chariot horses; ~0.06-0.12 per inhabitant.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: desert barriers, Nile supply, fortified frontier; 1.3 for Nubian and Sinai approaches.

notes: Snapshot = c. 1450 BCE (low chronology), late reign of Thutmose III after the Megiddo (1457) and Euphrates (Year 33) campaigns. Forces = standing army at campaign start plus garrisons; no Egyptian army total survives. Ancient figures used only as anchors: 924 captured chariots at Megiddo (Karnak annals). Population convention: Egypt, Nubia and the Canaanite vassals inside the border.
